lessons.title: ಹನ್ನೊಂದು to ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು — numbers 11–20
lessons.gloss: 11-20 — additive "ten-echo" compounds for the teens, then ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು (20), compositionally "two-tens" from OLD Dravidian roots — though the pieces have shifted enough that it no longer looks like the MODERN words eraḍu/hattu on the surface

segments.text: You've now seen four different language families each build "twenty" as its own special, opaque word — Sanskrit's vimshati, Latin's viginti, Arabic's ʿishrūn. Kannada's twenty genuinely started life as "two tens" too — but be careful: the modern surface no longer shows it plainly.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: ಹನ್ನೊಂದು–ಹತ್ತೊಂಬತ್ತು — "ten" + digit

segments.text: Kannada's teens are built on ಹತ್ತು (hattu, "ten") plus each digit — ಹನ್ನೊಂದು (hannondu, 11), ಹನ್ನೆರಡು (hanneraḍu, 12), and onward through ಹತ್ತೊಂಬತ್ತು (hattombattu, 19). Each teen is a compound built the same way English builds "four-teen" — just placed the same digit-plus-ten pattern in front instead of behind.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು — "two-tens" underneath, but not on the surface anymore

segments.text: ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು (ippattu, "twenty") traces back to Proto-Dravidian ir- ("two") + paHtu ("ten") — a genuine compositional origin, "two-tens." But be honest about what's actually visible today: the ir- piece is an old bound root, not the same as modern Kannada's everyday word for "two," ಎರಡು (eraḍu) — a separate, longer descendant of the same ancient family. And the "ten" piece surfaces here as -pp- (geminated after the r), not as modern ಹತ್ತು (hattu)'s h- — because Kannada's historical p becomes h shift only fired at the start of a word, and this "ten" sits in the middle of the compound, so it never lenited. So ippattu really did start as "two-tens" — you just can't spot modern eraḍu or modern hattu inside it anymore the way you might expect. Compare this to Sanskrit's विंशति (vimshati), Latin's vīgintī, and Arabic's عشرون (ʿishrūn): those have no compositional "two-ten" origin at all, not even a buried one — a genuinely different kind of history from Kannada's.

segments.instruction: "ippattu" — twenty, "two-tens" underneath, from the OLD ir-/ paHtu roots, not directly from hattu/eraḍu
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ippattu" — twenty, "two-tens" underneath, from the OLD *ir-/ *paHtu roots, not directly from hattu/eraḍu]

segments.text: How are Kannada's teens built? (ಹತ್ತು (ten) + a digit, compounded.) Does ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು (twenty) have a compositional "two-tens" origin? (Yes — Proto-Dravidian ir- "two" + paHtu "ten.") Can you still spot modern eraḍu or modern hattu inside it today? (No — the old bound "two" root and the un-lenited middle-of-word "ten" root look different from their modern standalone descendants.) Do Sanskrit's vimshati or Latin's vīgintī have any compositional origin like this at all? (No — neither has a buried "two-ten" history the way Kannada's does.)

lessons.title: ನನಗೆ — one ending, and the sentences that have no subject
lessons.gloss: second pass over the suffix that carries knowing, wanting and age alike — and the sentence built with no subject at all

segments.text: Say that you know Kannada. Then say that you speak it. Only one of the two sentences has a subject — say which.
ನನಗೆ ಕನ್ನಡ ಗೊತ್ತು (nanage kannaḍa gottu) is to-me Kannada known. There is no I in it and no verb to know: knowing is something that is the case for you, not something you do.

That one idea runs much further than it looks, and age is where it surfaces again. Kannada asks your age how-much? rather than how old are you — the years are a quantity attached to a person, not a property the person performs. The same suffix, the same shape of thought:

utterances: what you mean: I know Kannada. how Kannada builds it: to-me Kannada known.
what you mean: how old are you. how Kannada builds it: your age how-much.

segments.text: English needs a different verb for each — know, be — and Kannada needs neither.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one suffix per job

segments.text: Where Latin fuses number and case into one ending you cannot take apart, Kannada adds one visible suffix per job, and they stack in order. A reader who can find the seams can read a long word they have never met.

segments.instruction: that you speak Kannada, with its subject — nānu kannaḍa mātanāḍuttēne
segments.source: [YOU SAY: that you speak Kannada, with its subject — *nānu kannaḍa mātanāḍuttēne*]

segments.instruction: that you know it, without one — nanage kannaḍa gottu
segments.source: [YOU SAY: that you know it, without one — *nanage kannaḍa gottu*]

segments.instruction: that it is no trouble — paravāgilla
segments.source: [YOU SAY: that it is no trouble — *paravāgilla*]

segments.text: Which of the two sentences about Kannada has no subject? (The one about knowing.) How many jobs does a single Kannada suffix do? (One — they stack rather than fuse.)

lessons.title: ಹವಾಮಾನ (havāmāna) — a genuine two-language hybrid word
lessons.gloss: weather — a Persian+Sanskrit HYBRID compound: hava ("air," from Persian/Arabic) + maana ("measure," Sanskrit)

segments.text: Kannada's word for "weather" isn't purely Sanskrit or purely native — it's a compound with a piece from each of two different borrowed sources.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: ಹವಾಮಾನ — "air-measure," a hybrid compound

segments.text: ಹವಾಮಾನ (havāmāna) = "weather" — built from two pieces:
ಹವಾ (hava, "air") — itself a loanword, from Persian هوا (havā), which traces back to Arabic هَوَاء (hawāʾ, "air"). This is the exact same root behind Hindi's own हवा (havā, "air, wind").
ಮಾನ (māna, "measure") — from Sanskrit मान (māna), "measure, standard" (the same word behind pramāṇa, "proof, measure of truth").
So havāmāna literally means "air-measure" — and it's genuinely a two-source hybrid, not a single borrowed compound: one piece Perso-Arabic, one piece Sanskrit, fused into one Kannada word.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: ಮಳೆ ಬರುತ್ತಿದೆ — "rain is coming"

segments.text: ಮಳೆ ಬರುತ್ತಿದೆ. — "It's raining." — literally "rain is coming." (maḷe baruttide.)

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "maḷe baruttide" — it's raining, "rain is coming"]

segments.text: What are the two pieces of ಹವಾಮಾನ, and where does each come from? (ಹವಾ, "air," a Persian/Arabic loan; ಮಾನ, "measure," native Sanskrit.) What does havāmāna literally mean? ("Air-measure.") What other Indian language shares the exact same word for "air"? (Hindi — havā.)

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Before the new word: say the last thing you learned, once, out loud.
ಝರಿ — jhari — "a stream".
Say it: jhari. Look at its shape as you say it: the next lesson takes one piece of it, ಝ, and writes it on its own.
What is "a stream"? (ಝರಿ, jhari.)

lessons.title: ಝ (jha) — one character, and the pattern it completes
lessons.gloss: the single character ಝ — the breathed partner of ಜ, completing a pattern you have met six times

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ಝ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ಊ — short or long?
One character this time, and it is the rarest one in this book. That is the reason to meet it now rather than inside a word.
ಝ — jha.
It is ಜ (ja) with a puff of breath behind it. Hold your palm at your mouth: on ja the air stays put, on jha it hits your hand.
You have met that pairing six times already, in letters you can read:
ಕ ka, ಖ kha.
ಗ ga, ಘ gha.
ಡ ḍa, ಢ ḍha.
ದ da, ಧ dha.
ಪ pa, ಫ pha.
ಬ ba, ಭ bha.
Two of those sit inside words you say daily — the ಧ of ಧನ್ಯವಾದ dhanyavāda, the ಭ of ಶುಭ śubha. ಝ (jha) takes the same step from ಜ, and its shape keeps the plain letter visible inside it.
Why it is rare. A native Kannada word will almost never hand you this letter. It writes words Kannada took in from elsewhere — and one of those is coming shortly, which is why you meet it here first.

blocks.title: Writing: ಝ — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on ಝ (jha) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
